## Discussion  {.smaller style="font-size: 0.75em;"}

::: smaller
**Rental stress is widespread — but geography matters**

- Nearly **60% of all listings** exceed the 30% affordability threshold nationally
- Queensland (75.1%) has the highest stress rate, yet NSW has the largest absolute number of stressed listings (1,678)
- This divergence shows stress *rates* and *volumes* tell different stories

**Income — not rent — is the key driver**

- The ACT has the **highest median rent** but the **lowest stress rate (11.7%)**
- Its substantially higher household income shields most renters from stress classification
- Reinforces the need for income-adjusted affordability measures

**Dwelling type creates a clear affordability gradient**

- Acreage/semi-rural: highest stress (88.2%), highest rent ($970/wk) — least accessible
- Houses (65.2%) and apartments (63.1%) — high stress despite being the most common types
- Studios: lowest stress (11.5%), lowest rent ($430/wk) — most accessible option
:::

---

## Conclusion & Recommendations {.smaller}

::: smaller
::: columns
::: {.column width="50%"}
**Key Takeaways**

- Nearly **3 in 5 listings** are unaffordable for a median-income household
- Queensland, WA, and Tasmania face the greatest proportional pressure
- Income is a **stronger affordability lever** than rent levels alone
- Rental unaffordability is both **widespread and structurally entrenched**

:::

::: {.column width="50%"}
**Recommendations**

🏛️ Expand Rent Assistance calibrated to state-level incomes

🏗️ Increase supply of studios and one-bedroom apartments through rezoning

🏘️ Build-to-rent schemes and social housing investment for mainstream dwellings

📊 Future research to incorporate suburb-level income and vacancy rate data

:::
